notes.text: Fry the tofu in three batches, and the vegetables in two, so the pan stays hot.

move.title: Thin, even, and fast
move.body: A stir-fry cooks in minutes over high heat, so everything has to be cut before the pan goes on. Today you'll julienne carrots and peppers into even matchsticks, crisp cubes of tofu in batches, then toss it all with a garlic-ginger sauce over rice.

callback.body: If you made fresh spring rolls, you've julienned carrots: flat side, planks, then matchsticks. In a stir-fry the size matters even more, because pieces of different thickness cook at different speeds in a hot pan.

why.title: Make a flat side first
why.body: A round carrot rolls under the knife. Slice a thin strip off one side and lay it on that flat side, and it sits still for every cut after.

why.title: Even matchsticks cook together
why.body: Heat reaches the middle of a thin piece faster than a thick one. Matchsticks all about ⅛ inch thick are tender-crisp at the same moment; a thick one stays raw while a thin one goes limp.

why.title: Press the tofu
why.body: Tofu is packed in water. Pressed under something heavy for 15 minutes, it gives some up, so it browns in the pan instead of steaming and spitting.

why.title: Cook in batches
why.body: Crowd a pan and the food drops its temperature, so it steams in its own water. A single layer with space around each piece keeps the pan hot and browns the outside.

why.title: Hard vegetables go in first
why.body: Carrots take longer than peppers, and snow peas take the least. Adding them in that order means they all finish together.

why.title: Garlic and ginger go in late
why.body: Minced garlic burns in under a minute in a hot pan and turns bitter. Added after the vegetables, for just 30 seconds before the sauce, it stays sweet and fragrant.

wrong.fix: The pan wasn't hot enough, or you moved it too soon. Wait until the oil shimmers, and turn the cubes only when they're golden and let go.
The pan was crowded, or they cooked too long. Next time, cook in two batches and take them out while they still snap.

wrong.sign: Some matchsticks are raw, some limp
wrong.fix: They were different thicknesses. Cut planks the same thickness first, and the sticks follow.
Stir the sauce again right before it goes in, because the cornstarch sinks. Let it bubble a full 30 seconds to thicken.

quiz.q: Why are the vegetables cut into even matchsticks?
choices: So they cook through at the same time
So they soak up more sauce
quiz.explain: Thin pieces cook faster than thick ones.

quiz.q: Why cook the tofu in batches?
choices: A crowded pan steams instead of browning
quiz.explain: A single layer keeps the pan hot.

quiz.q: Why do the garlic and ginger go in near the end?
choices: They burn fast and turn bitter
They need the least heat to be safe
quiz.explain: 30 seconds in a hot pan is enough.

steps.text: Put the rice in the saucepan and cover it with cold water. Swish it with your hand, then carefully pour off the cloudy water, holding the rice back with your hand. Do this 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the rice cooks up fluffy instead of gluey.

steps.text: Add the rice's {qty:water} of water. Bring it to a boil over high heat with the lid off. Then turn the heat to low, put the lid on, and cook without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: When the timer rings, turn off the burner and leave the lid on. The rice keeps steaming until you're ready.

steps.text: Drain the tofu, wrap it in paper towels and the kitchen towel, and set it on the plate. Put something heavy on top, like the skillet, and leave it.
steps.tip: Cut the vegetables while it presses.

steps.text: Peel the carrots and cut them into 3-inch pieces. Slice a thin strip off one side of each piece and lay it on that flat side. Slice it the long way into planks about ⅛ inch thick.
Stack 2 or 3 planks and julienne them: slice the stack the long way into matchsticks ⅛ inch wide. Put them in the medium bowl.
steps.look: Matchsticks all about the same thickness, like a thin pencil lead.
steps.tip: Hold the stack with the claw, knuckles against the blade.

steps.text: Cut the top and bottom off the pepper. Stand it up, cut down one side, and open it out flat. Cut away the core and white ribs. Lay it skin side down and julienne it into strips ⅛ inch wide. Add them to the bowl.
steps.tip: Skin side down, the knife doesn't skid on the shiny skin.

steps.text: Snap the stem end off each snow pea and pull the string down the side. Keep them in a pile next to the bowl.
Slice the green onions thin. Peel and mince the garlic. Grate the ginger on the small holes of the grater. Put them together in the small bowl.
In the liquid measuring cup, stir together the soy sauce, the sauce's water, the honey, rice vinegar, cornstarch, and sesame oil with the fork.
Unwrap the tofu and cut it into ¾-inch cubes. Toss them gently on the plate with the tofu's cornstarch and the salt.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add half the tofu in one layer, with space between the cubes. Turn them with the spatula as each side turns golden, then move them to the plate.
steps.look: Golden and crisp on most sides.

steps.text: Add another tablespoon of oil and cook the rest of the tofu the same way. Move it to the plate.
Add the last tablespoon of oil. Add the carrots and stir-fry, tossing every few seconds, for 2 minutes. Add the pepper and snow peas and stir-fry 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Bright in color and tender, but still with a snap.

steps.text: Push the vegetables to the sides. Add the green onions, garlic, and ginger to the middle and stir them for 30 seconds.
steps.look: It smells strong; the garlic hasn't browned.

steps.text: Stir the sauce again and pour it in. Add the tofu back. Toss everything until the sauce bubbles and turns glossy.
steps.look: The sauce is thick enough to coat the vegetables.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Fluff the rice with the fork and serve the stir-fry over it.
